newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cargill and Ceval deny rumors of Brazil takeover.
newsitem.headline: Cargill and Ceval deny rumors of Brazil takeover.

text.p: U.S. grains giant Cargill Inc and Brazilian processor Ceval Alimentos declined to comment Friday about market rumors that Cargill had bought either part or all of Ceval's operations in Brazil.

"We have no information about this," said a spokesman for Ceval, referring all further inquiries to Cargill. "These types of rumors have cropped up in the past and it's been very damaging for us," he added.
"As a matter of policy, we don't comment on rumors," said Linda Thrane at Cargill's public affairs office in Minneapolis, Minnesota.
The spokesmen were responding to rumors in the North American cash grain trade and local stock circles.
"I've heard that Cargill accountants have been sitting in the offices at Ceval all week," said one U.S. trader with clients in Brazil.
Ceval's preferred shares closed up 4.44 percent at 14.10 reais ($13.05) on the rumor, following a 10 percent increase in the stock price Thursday.
The Sao Paulo stock exchange said it had not received any statement from Ceval.

Caspian Securities analyst Lilyanna Young said Ceval's dominant participation in the Brazilian soybean market would provide a good launching point into the Brazilian market for either Cargill or Archer Daniels Midland Co.

"The company denied the rumors, but a takeover does make sense as Ceval is highly indebted (net debt equity ratio of 83 percent in December 1996) and has presented very narrow margins," Young said in a daily market report.

"However, the acquisition of only the soybean activities seems unlikely as it would devaluate the company's meat operations (28 percent of Ceval's total revenues, or $700 million) due to its vertically integrated production," she said.
There was talk that in the event of a 100 percent purchase, Cargill would look to swap Ceval's meat operations with processor Sadia, said a Brazilian soybean trader.

A veteran CBOT trader who handles South American clients said he would not be surprised to see Cargill build up its presence in Brazil after ADM in May agreed to buy Glencore Grain Holding's grain handling facilities in Brazil and Paraguay.

"Cargill has been known to make acquisitions for strategic purposes and even for defensive purposes," the trader said. "With ADM increasing its presence in South America, it makes sense for Cargill to try to counter."
